title: Protocol for Small Mustelid Carcass Collection, Handling, and Storage
author: Andrin C. Dürst
materials: Use clean, sterilized tools (scissors, scalpel, forceps).
Taxon code Standardized codes for taxon codes include:
Use durable, waterproof and ethanol-proof labels .

steps.title: Prepare for Collection
steps.instruction: Ensure all necessary safety and hygiene equipment is available.

substeps.instruction: Wear disposable gloves when handling carcasses; if unavailable, use a plastic bag turned inside out as an improvised glove.
Have hand sanitizer and hand-washing facilities available for use after handling.

steps.title: Collect Carcass and Field Data
steps.instruction: Secure the specimen and record essential metadata at the site of discovery.

substeps.instruction: Place the carcass into a plastic bag and tie it closed with a secure knot.
Place the first bag into a second plastic bag and tie it closed (double-bagging).
Insert a label or note containing the label ID, date, and GPS coordinates (preferably WGS84) between the two bags.

Record essential data: GPS coordinates, date of collection, species identification/certainty, cause of death (confirmed or assumed), carcass condition (fresh, decomposed, scavenged, etc.), finder's name/contact, habitat notes, and optional photographs.

steps.title: Transport to Coordinator
steps.instruction: Move the specimen to the local collection coordinator as quickly as possible.

substeps.instruction: Keep the carcass cool in a cool box or refrigerator until delivery (ideally same day or overnight).

If using a courier: send in the afternoon just before the parcel drop-off deadline for next-day delivery; avoid sending before weekends; use cool packs and/or insulated packaging (e.g., bubble wrap, multiple paper layers).
If transfer is delayed and cooling is impossible, freeze the carcass as a last resort after consulting the coordinator, provided no pathogen analysis is planned.

steps.title: Initial Processing and Morphometrics
steps.instruction: Perform initial identification and measurements upon receipt.

substeps.instruction: Assign a unique label ID using the format: [CountryCode]-[Year]-[InstitutionCode]-[TaxonCode]-[SampleType]-[SampleNumber][LetterSuffix].
Take morphological measurements.
Determine sex (male/female) and age class (juvenile, subadult, adult).

steps.title: Tissue Sampling for Genetic Analysis
steps.instruction: Extract and preserve tissue samples before freezing the carcass.

substeps.instruction: Select tissue source: tongue (recommended for ease), back muscle (via ventral cavity), or heart muscle (preferred for genetic analysis but less accessible).
If the carcass is intended for taxidermy, sample from non-visible areas (e.g., tongue).
Cut small pieces (minimum 0.5–1 cm³).
Immediately preserve samples in screw-cap microcentrifuge tubes filled with >95% ethanol (preferably 99%).
Use ethanol-proof ink or pencil for labels.
Store tissue samples at -20 °C or lower for long-term preservation.

steps.title: Pathogen Sampling
steps.instruction: Collect samples for disease or pathogen analysis if planned.

substeps.instruction: Perform sampling or hand the carcass to veterinary specialists before freezing to ensure pathogen viability.

steps.title: Long-term Carcass Storage
steps.instruction: Freeze the carcass for preservation if no further immediate analysis is required.

substeps.instruction: Ensure the carcass is double-bagged with clear labeling on the outer bag (sample ID, date, and location).
Store frozen at a minimum of -20 °C (preferably -80 °C).
Avoid thawing and refreezing cycles.

steps.title: Database Management
steps.instruction: Maintain a digital record of all specimens and samples.

substeps.instruction: Maintain a secure, backed-up digital database with metadata: Unique sample ID, Date/time of collection, GPS coordinates (WGS84), Species identification/certainty, Cause of death, Condition, Collector name/contact, Storage location, Morphometrics, and Comments/photos.
Ensure database entries match physical labels exactly.
Update the database whenever samples are moved, processed, or used.
